title: 6  Biographies of Dǒng, Two Yuán, Liú
text:
Dǒng Zhuó also has a biography in Hòu Hàn shū 72.↩︎
Vigilantes (xià) were individuals of martial abilities who followed their own justice. Compare with European knight-errants or Japanese rōnin.↩︎
The six prefectures of Lǒngxī, Tiānshuǐ, Āndìng, Běidì, Shàngjùn, and Xīhé formed the northwestern border of the Hàn Empire. Feather Forest (yǔlín) was a division of the Imperial guard in the capital city.↩︎
This is to mean that Dǒng Zhuó could shoot a bow from either hand while riding.↩︎
An army (jūn) was commanded by a General (jiāngjūn), with a Major (sīmǎ) serving as the General’s chief of staff for military affairs.↩︎
Zhào Yāng was a Spring and Autumn era minister of Jìn state. He mobilized an army at his stronghold at Jìnyáng city and took custody over the Duke of Jìn, framing his coup not as treason but as fulfilling a duty to purge evil ministers surrounding his ruler.↩︎
Metal Mace Bearer (zhíjīnwú) was in charge of security and policing the capital city.↩︎
The Yellow Gates (huángmén) department consisted of eunuch officials serving in the restricted areas of the Palace, so named for the yellow gates that marked the areas.↩︎
Witch rebels (yāozéi) were rebels said to deceive and bewitch the masses.↩︎
This is an idiom to mean one is still young, having many years (springs and autumns) ahead of them.↩︎
The Yǒnglè Dowager Empress, family name Dǒng, called by her residence in Yǒnglè Palace, was the mother of Hàn Emperor Líng. After Emperor Líng’s death, Emperor Líng’s Empress, family name Hé, took power as Dowager and quickly moved to eliminate her potentially dangerous political rival. The Dowager Dǒng and Dǒng Zhuó were from other sides of the empire and not related.↩︎
This is a physiognomy term for the head, referring to a wide jaw (low) and narrow forehead (high).↩︎
Investigator (dūyóu) was a prefecture position, in charge of the postal relay stations within the prefecture, and of investigating and impeaching local officials.↩︎
Enlightened office (míngfǔ) was a term of address for a prefecture administrator.↩︎
Individuals can refer to themselves by their own personal name as a sign of humility.↩︎
This was a form of execution where the victim had their four limbs and head tied to five chariots and was then pulled apart, reserved for the most heinous crimes.↩︎
Grand Preceptor (tàishī) was the most senior of the Three Excellencies position used by Zhōu. It was restored here to honor Dǒng Zhuó with an exceptional position above the Excellencies. Shàngfù was an honorific previously used to honor the Zhōu dynasty Grand Preceptor Tàigōng Wàng, and therefore interpreted to mean something like a father figure for the Emperor.↩︎
Grand Scribe (tàishǐ) was responsible for record-keeping, which also included the recording and interpretation of omens such as atmospheric auras.↩︎
The omen could refer to Dǒng Zhuó himself, so he wished to have another senior minister killed to fulfill the omen to avoid having it applied to himself.↩︎
To mean that people were too afraid to speak to one another.↩︎
Coins of the time were circular, with a square hole at the center. The inner and outer rims would normally have defined border edges to prevent coin clipping.↩︎
Pán Gēng was a king of the Shāng/Yīn dynasty. Three chapters preserved in the Shàng Shū are attributed to him.↩︎
Guānzhōng ”Inside the Passes” refers to the Wèi river valley, named for the surrounding mountains and mountain passes. It had been the heartland of Qín state.↩︎
Hán Yuē was another personal name of Hán Suì.↩︎
The count of eleven is achieved by not including Emperors that were retroactively declared illegitimate. The count also does not include the two founding Emperors Gāozǔ and Guāng-Wǔ, which would lead to the more commonly cited twelve reigns.↩︎
The title Shí Bāo Shì Chèn can be interpreted as ”Prophecies of the Stone Bud Room.” During Hàn there were various apocryphal prophecy texts in circulation. Almost none are extant except for quotations and references in other works.↩︎
Gēngshǐ ”Another Beginning” was a title used by Liú Xuán, who attempted to declare a restoration of Hàn with himself as Emperor. The Chìméi ”Red Eyebrows” was a large rebel group, named for painting their foreheads red to identify themselves, which killed Liú Xuán and devastated Cháng’ān.↩︎
Lǒngyòu ”Right of Lǒng mountain” was a prefecture and general region in the northwest, known for its timber.↩︎
The Great Carriage (dàjià) was one of the formal carriages of the Emperor, and also used as a euphemism to refer to the Emperor.↩︎
Yīn refers to the feminine/earth/dark/cold/low principle in contrast to the masculine/heaven/light/hot/high Yáng principle in Yīn-Yáng duality.↩︎
In formal Court dress, officials would use writing brush pens as hairpins in their headgear in order to be able to write notes and draft government documents at any time.↩︎
Huángfǔ Sōng’s appellation (zì).↩︎
The fènghuáng is a mythical bird considered the king of birds. The term is sometimes translated as ”phoenix” but the fènghuáng does not have the same associations of cyclical rebirth through fire as the phoenix myth.↩︎
During Hàn, one lǐ was about 415 meters, 260 lǐ would be about 108 kilometers.↩︎
Thousand (千), lǐ (里), and grass (艸) together form the character Dǒng (董). Ten (十), day (日), and divination (卜) form the character Zhuó (卓).↩︎
A talisman for warding off weapons (bì bīng fú) was a magical charm to protect against weapons.↩︎
Axe and block were tools for execution, placing the victim’s head atop the block and then cutting the head off with the axe.↩︎
Stalk divination (shì) was an ancient divination practice of using yarrow stalks to generate random numbers to select one of the sixty-four hexagrams.↩︎
The trigram Lí (☲) is associated with fire, the trigram duì with metal (☱). Lí on top of Duì forms the hexagram gé (䷰).↩︎
A wolf’s mat (lángjí) was a metaphor for total chaos and disorder, based on a folk belief that wolves left a trampled mess wherever they stopped in order to not be tracked.↩︎
Chíyáng county was in Zuǒpíngyí.↩︎
Měiyáng county was in Yòufúfēng.↩︎
Wànnián county was in Zuǒpíngyí.↩︎
Píngyáng county was in Hédōng.↩︎
To create power (zuò wēi) and to create fortune (zuò fú) is an idiom for the authority of the ruler to order deaths and spare lives.↩︎
The Management Office (yùfǔ) was the Imperial Palace’s internal treasury and storehouse.↩︎
The Six Dīng (liù dīng) were the Dào spirits Dīngmǎo, Dīngsì, Dīngwèi, Dīngyǒu, Dīnghài, Dīngchǒu, believed to be used by the God of Heaven to perform labors, and therefore that Dào priests could summon them to perform tasks.↩︎
Talismen impeachments (fúhé) were similar to the actual talismen (fú) carried by messengers to verify the authenticity of orders, but instead used to give orders to spirits. Amulets (yāshèng) were magic items said to be able to suppress (yā) and overcome (shèng) other magic influences.↩︎
Ruthless enforcers (gěngdú) can be interpreted more literally as ‘bone stuck in the throat’ (gěng) and ‘poison’ (dú).↩︎
The term hǎojué originally referred to a fine alcohol goblet, and by extension came to refer to high office with generous salary.↩︎
Capped and girdled (guāndài) refer to the gentry class.↩︎
The Báibō ”white waves” was a bandit confederation.↩︎
Chángbó was originally a Zhōu office title, but by Hàn had become a metaphorical term to refer to the Emperor’s attendants, such as the Attendant Centrals or Regular Attendants.↩︎
Curtains wéiwò refer to the inner rooms of the Imperial Palace.↩︎
Dà Sīmǎ was an irregularly used title for a supreme commander of all military forces.↩︎
Here right is the same as above, left as below.↩︎
Traditionally high appointments involved the candidate ritually declining and suggesting another candidate. This was an expected ritual display of humility, but may have also served a practical purpose of giving time to build and confirm a consensus before finalizing an appointment.↩︎
Central Palace [zhōng gōng] refers to the Empress.↩︎
Yuán Shào also has a biography in Hòu Hàn shū 74.↩︎
Hàn Emperor Míng, personal name Liú Zhuāng, regined 57 - 75 AD, Annals in Hòu Hàn shū 2.↩︎
Emperor Míng’s younger brother Liú Yīng, the King of Chǔ, was charged with plotting treason in late 70 to early 71 AD, leading to his removal as King and eventually his suicide. Chǔ kingdom was converted to Chǔ prefecture, and a large number of implicated individuals were arrested and investigated. As the Chǔ prefecture Administrator reviewing the legal cases, Yuán Ān was able to save the lives of many of the imprisoned.↩︎
Hàn Emperor Zhāng, personal name Liú Dá, reigned 75 - 88 AD, Annals in Hòu Hàn shū 3.↩︎
In Hàn traditions, adoption was done in order to main ancestral sacrifices, and therefore usually done within the same male-line clan to maintain lineages that had gone extinct. Here Yuán Chéng’s line had gone extinct so Yuán Féng had Yuán Shào adopted over to nominally continue his elder brother’s lineage.↩︎
During the final decades of Hàn, the government was dominated by the powerful clans that married with the Imperial family, usually in the form of child Emperors controlled by a regency of their mother or stepmother Dowager Empress and her clan relatives. Perhaps the most notorious of these was Liáng Jì (88 - 159 AD), who came to power through his younger sister the Empress Liáng. See the biography of Liáng Jì in Hòu Hàn shū 34.↩︎
The capping ceremony (ruòguàn) marked the transition to adulthood, when a boy received the headdress of an adult. During Hàn, Púyáng county was in Hédōng prefecture. A county with a population less than ten thousand households was governed by a Chief (zhǎng) instead of the usual Magistrate (lìng).↩︎
In traditional mourning ritual, an individual observes a nominal three years mourning period for each parent. In practice “three years” did not necessarily mean thirty-six months, but here Yuán Shào was likely making a calculated political withdrawal from government service.↩︎
For Zhāng Miǎo see the biography of Lǚ Bù in Sān Guó zhì 7. For Hé Yóng see Hòu Hàn shū 67. Wú Zǐqīng is no longer known, but he may have been the Wú Shuò. For Xǔ Yōu see later in the biography of Yuán Shào. For Wǔ Qióng see the biography of Dǒng Zhuó.↩︎
Death Squad (sǐshì) refers to individuals said to be unafraid of death and willing to undertake suicidal missions in service of their sponsor. A private individual not accepting recruitments to government positions while raising a private army would naturally fall under suspicion of plotting treason.↩︎
Here Péi Sōngzhī notes that observing a mourning period for a parent so late after the fact has no basis in Ritual canon. This is perhaps further evidence that Yuán Shào was using a nominal claim of mourning for a calculated political withdrawal.↩︎
The Yǒnglè Dowager Empress, called for Yǒnglè Palace, was the mother of Hàn Emperor Líng.↩︎
The eunuchs employed in the Yellow Gates and Regular Attendants had dominated the government during the reigns of Hàn Emperors Huán and Líng. Previously, Hàn Emperor Huán had empowered the eunuchs to use them in a coup against his overly powerful regent Liáng Jì. Emperor Huán later died without an heir, leading to the posthumous adoption and enthronment of a distant cousin, Emperor Líng, under the regency of the Dowager Empress Dòu and her father Dòu Wǔ. Dòu Wǔ planned to purge the eunuchs, but the plan leaked and the eunuchs struck first, purging Dòu Wǔ and maintaining their dominant positions under Emperor Líng.↩︎
The Five Camps (wǔ yíng) was the regular standing army at the capital city Luòyáng.↩︎
Central people (zhōng rén) refers to the people in control of the Palace, in this case the eunuchs.↩︎
Hé Jìn was the elder half-brother of the Dowager Empress Hé, mother of the Emperor.↩︎
The other office may refer to the Dowager Empress Hé’s other half brother Hé Miáo, who held office as Chariots and Cavalry General. Hé Jìn and the Dowager shared the same father, Hé Miáo and the Dowager the same mother, but Hé Miáo was adopted over to the Hé family and took the Hé surname.↩︎
Shēn Bó, or ”Earl of Shēn,” was a celebrated relative by marriage of the Zhōu dynasty’s ruling family, maternal uncle of Zhōu King Xuān.↩︎
Greatly Departed (dà xíng) refers to the recently deceased Emperor, before the posthumous name is determined. At this time Emperor Líng had recently died and his body was in the Palace Front Hall, though the posthumous name Líng had not yet been selected.↩︎
Horizontal saber deep salute (héng dāo cháng yī) was a deep standing bow with both hands clasped together and extended forward, while keeping one’s sword or saber horizontal across the body.↩︎
Kàng village was in Yǐngchuān. See the annotations to Hòu Hàn shū 74.↩︎
The then-Emperor Liú Biàn was born from the Empress, his younger brother the King of Chénliú Liú Xié was born from a concubine.↩︎
The translation ‘stubbornly defiant’ assumes that the text’s qū jiāng is an equivalent to jué jiàng (倔強)↩︎
This refers to Yuán Shào by his office as Chariots and Cavalry General (chēqí jiāngjūn)↩︎
Shì is an honorific used to avoid Yuán Shào’s personal name out of respect.↩︎
Chief Clerk (zhǎngshǐ) was the chief of staff for a high official. Separate Carriage (biéijià) and Manager Central (zhìzhōng) were the two highest provincial staff officers under the provincial Governor.↩︎
Yuán Shào is interpreting the Year Name Chūpíng “Beginning of Pacification” as “(Běn)chū pacifies.”↩︎
Eight Kitchens (bāchú) may be to mean that they “fed” society through their charity and righteousness.↩︎
Liú Xiàng (77 - 6 BC) was a Western Hàn era scholar.↩︎
Smearing blood on drums (xìn gǔ) was an ancient war ritual where the blood of some sacrifice was smeared onto war drums, to pray for good fortune in battle.↩︎
Tàishān Fǔjūn is a god of Tài Mountain, Hébó a god of the Hé, or Yellow River.↩︎
Guǎngzōng was in Jùlù prefecture.↩︎
Ivory Gates (yámén) were ivory tipped flags that marked military camp entrances.↩︎
Chìqiū county was in Wèi prefecture.↩︎
These bandit leaders all used rather stylistic sobriquets rather than formal names. A direct translation of these might be Yú the Poison, Zuǒ Eight-zhàng-mustache, Liú the Rock, Qīng Oxhorn or Green Oxhorn, Yellow Dragon, Zuǒ Colonel or Left Colonel, Guō the Great Worthy, Lǐ Big Eyes, Yú the Root (though it has also been proposed Yúdīgēn may instead be a phonetic transcription of a foreign name.)↩︎
When the two officers quarreled, Hàn Emperor Guǎng-Wǔ had both summoned to his presence, and had them leave in the same carriage. The story is in the biography of Kòu Xún in Hòu Hàn shū 16.↩︎
The current Emperor Liú Xié had been enthroned by Dǒng Zhuó over Yuán Shào’s opposition.↩︎
Yuán Shào uses the first person pronoun gū ”orphaned,” or ”fatherless.” This pronoun was historically used by vassal lords, as usually their noble titles would be inherited from a deceased father.↩︎
Overall Supervisor (dūdū) was a military supervisor in control over a certain region. Inspector (cìshǐ) was the actual head of a province.↩︎
Temple Victory (miàoshèng) refers to the concept of achieving victory from the overall strategic planning in the Temple.↩︎
Huángshígōng ”Yellow Stone Elder” was a reclusive figure during the Qín-Hàn transition period said to have taught military strategy to Zhāng Liáng.↩︎
The Second Emperor of Qín was weak, allowing the powerful Chancellor Zhào Gāo to seize control. The Shàng Shū has a quote of ”create authority create fortune” as exclusive prerogatives of the ruler, referring respectively to the ruler’s authority to issue punishments and rewards. Eventually Zhào Gāo sent troops to attack Wàngyí Palace to force the Emperor to commit suicide.↩︎
After the death of Hàn Emperor Gāo Liú Bāng, his widow the Empress Lǚ took control of the government, greatly empowering her clansmen Lǚ Lù and Lǚ Chǎn.↩︎
The Restricted Ministries (shěngjīn) referred to the government offices within the Imperial Palace.↩︎
‘The below rising to replace the above’ (xià líng shàng tì) is a quote from the Zuǒ Zhuàn.↩︎
After the death of Empress Lǚ, the Marquess of Jiàng Zhōu Bó along with the Marquess of Zhūxū Liú Zhāng (a grandson of Hàn Emperor Gāo Liú Bāng) led a military coup to overthrow the Lǚ clan and invite Liú Héng, another son of Liú Bāng, to become Emperor. Liú Héng later received the posthumous name Hàn Emperor Wén and the Temple Name Tàizōng.↩︎
Tripod managers (dǐng sī) refer to the Three Excellencies through the analogy of the tripod having three legs↩︎
Tent Office (mùfǔ) refers to the tents of the commanding military officer. In this case Yuán Shào uses it as a first person pronoun for himself. Japan also famously adopted the term Tent Office as Bakufu, along with the term General (jiāngjūn) as Shogun, to refer to their Shogunate↩︎
Falcons rising (yīng yáng) is a metaphor for military commanders.↩︎
Hawks and hounds (yīngquán) and claws and teeth (zhǎoyá) are both metaphors for hired thugs and lackeys.↩︎
This is a reference to the Spring and Autumn era Qín commander Mèngmíng Shì. He suffered a humiliating defeat against Jìn but was pardoned, and repaid the generous treatment he received with a great victory.↩︎
Yáng Biāo successively served in all three positions of the Three Excellencies.↩︎
Liú Wǔ, posthumously Liáng King Xiào was a full younger brother of Hàn Emperor Jǐng. See Hàn shū 47 and Shǐjì 58.↩︎
The term xiāoxióng refers to an individual of ambitious and ruthless character. Compare similar terms yīngxióng “outstanding hero” and jiànxiōng “treacherous opportunist,” where xióng “hero” should be understood in the classical sense of an individual of great strength and ability, without any particular comment on morality.↩︎
Zhōnghuáng Bó was a legendary warrior of antiqutiy, Xià Yù and Wū Huò were legendary warriors from the Warring States era.↩︎
Horn (jiǎo) and drag (jǐ) refer to a strategy of attacking front and rear using the metaphor of hunting a beast by engaging its horns at the front and dragging its legs from the rear. Yuān and Shè counties were in Nányáng prefecture. The characters for the names are also commonly pronounced Wǎn and Yè in modern times, but the older readings are favored here, especially to disambiguate Yuān county from the Wǎn county in Lújiāng prefecture.↩︎
For Chén Lín see the biography of Wáng Càn in Sān Guó zhì 21.↩︎
The term for massacre (kēng) later also gained another meaning of “bury alive,” but does not have that meaning here.”↩︎
At this time Cáo Cāo was Governor of Yǎn Province (yǎnzhōu) and therefore referred to by his office.↩︎
Jī was the ruling family of the declining Zhōu dynasty, Yíng the ruling family of Qín state which eventually conquered the rival six states to establish the Qín Empire.↩︎
Field Allocations (fēnyě) refers to the astrological process of mapping regions of the sky to regions of the earth. Here it refers to the fate and fortune that Jū Shòu and Cáo Cāo should have ended up in different places.↩︎
This refers to Yuán Shào by his office title as Governor of Jì Province (jìzhōu)↩︎
Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng were celebrated strategists who served Liú Bāng at the initial rise of Hàn.↩︎
This refers to the fact that Yuán Shào was not an Emperor, so Tián Fēng was morally permitted to leave him.↩︎
A sortie gate (tūmén) was a smaller gate in the city walls used by the defenders to send out sorties for surprise attacks and raids against besiegers.↩︎
Qīng Yíng ”Blue Flies” is a song in the Shī jīng. Blue flies are a metaphor for slanderers spreading contamination through their accusations.↩︎
According to the Gōngyáng Zhuàn, Duke Zhuāng Fourth Year, Duke Xiāng of Qí destroyed Jǐ state to avenge a nine generation blood feud.↩︎
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn Duke Xiāng Nineteenth Year, after the Jìn state military commander Xún Yǎn died, the deputy commander Shì Gài took it upon himself to complete Xún Yǎn’s work in attacking the campaign against Qí state.↩︎
Bóyóu was the appellation of Xún Yǎn.↩︎
Xuān-zǐ was the posthumous name of Shì Gài.↩︎
Yuán Shàng is referred to by his office as Governor of Jì Province (jìzhōu).↩︎
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn Duke Yǐn Inaugural Year, Jiāng-shì plotted against her elder son Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng, attempting to replace him with her younger son.↩︎
Chónghuá was the personal name of Shùn, one of the Five Emperors. His younger brother Xiàng resented and repeatedly plotted against him.↩︎
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn Duke Yǐn Inaugural Year, after defeating his mother’s plot against him, Duke Zhuāng swore he would never see his mother again until they reached the underworld. Later he regretted this, and they met again in the Great Tunnel, the underground passage way into a tomb, to technically fulfill his oath while also allowing a reconciliation.↩︎
È Bó and Shí Shěn were two legendary figures from high antiquity, said to be brothers that warred for a long time until they were separated to opposite ends of hte world. See the Zuǒ Zhuàn Duke Zhāo Inaugural Year.↩︎
Chángdì is a song in the Shī jīng, ‘death and mourning’ (sǐ sàng) a line in the lyrics, singing that brothers must stand together in times of crisis.↩︎
This refers to Yuán Tán by his office as Inspector of Qīng Province (qīngzhōu cìshǐ).↩︎
Hán Lú and Dōngguō were legendary hunting dogs of antiquity. A parable tells that the two chased a hare, exhausting themselves, allowing a bystander farmer to reap the reward of their effort.↩︎
Zhōu-gōng suppressed the rebellions of his own brothers Guǎn and Cài.↩︎
Jìyǒu arranged for his own relative Zhēnshū to be poisoned for plotting against the ruling family.↩︎
At some point Yuán Tán was adopted over to continue the lineage of Yuán Shào’s elder brother, making him a legal nephew rather than son of Yuán Shào. This process involved a ritual declaration in the family ancestral shrines to inform the ancestors, and a record of the adoption in the family geneological records.↩︎
Yuán Shàng observed the highest level of mourning, wearing the mourning clothes called zhǎnshuāi, and resided in the ritual mourning hut near the grave, while Yuán Tán observed a lesser form of mourning. This reflected Yuán Tán’s changed status as a legal nephew rather than son of Yuán Shào.↩︎
This is a reference to a story of an art competition. Painters competed to see who could draw a snake the fastest. The first to finish had beaten the others so quickly that he then drew legs on the snake, but the second to finish then claimed the prize by arguing that snakes did not have legs.↩︎
The word for fraternal here is Kǒnghuái “deep yearning,” a quote from the Shījīng: “Brothers in deep yearning” (xiōngdì kǒnghuái).↩︎
Standing like a crane (qǐ zhǒng hè lì) is a visual metaphor for eager anticipation and desire.↩︎
The jade ring (huán) and jade pendant (jué) could be used in diplomacy to convey intentions. The complete ring indicated a wish to return and reconcile. The pendant was a notched incomplete ring, representing a definitive break and determination to fight.↩︎
Mǎ Mìdī was already being sent east on a broader mission to restore contact with the eastern warlords.↩︎
The prefecture unit containing the capital city was governed by an Intendant (yǐn) isntead of the usual Administrator (tàishǒu). Yuán Shù was also renaming Jiǔjiāng to Huáinán (meaning “south of the Huái river”).↩︎
The Suburb Sacrifices were an Imperial prerogative.↩︎
“On the street high” (dāngtúgāo) was a phrase circulated in apocryphal prophecy texts as early as Western Hàn, and Hàn Emperor Guāng-Wŭ referenced the prophecy in a letter to rival warlord Gōngsūn Shù to try to dissuade him from claiming Imperial title during the warlord period of the Western Hàn-Xīn-Eastern Hàn transition. Yuán Shù believed he fulfilled this prophecy because his name Shù has an ancient meaning of road, and the lù in his appellation Gōnglù can mean road. In fact, “on the street high” would be fulfilled by Wèi: an ancient meaning of the word Wèi is a two-tower gate over a road, which is “on the street high.”↩︎
Office Lord (fǔjūn) was the term of address to a prefecture administrator (tàishǒu).↩︎
Bó Yí and Shū Qí were famous figures during the Shāng-Zhōu transition who starved themselves to death in protest of Zhōu coming to power through military conquest.↩︎
Lǔyáng county was in Nányáng prefecture.↩︎
Huáróng county was in Nán prefecture.↩︎
Yíchéng county was in Nán prefecture.↩︎
Zhōnglú county was in Nán prefecture.↩︎
Xiāngyáng county was in Nán prefecture.↩︎
Section and phrase (zhāng jù) commentaries were pedagogical exegesis explaining classical texts.↩︎
Huáróng county was in Nán prefecture.↩︎
Here Liú Biǎo is referred to by his office as Governor of Jīng Province (jīngzhōu).↩︎
Minister of Staff (guānglùxūn), one of the Nine Minsiters, was in charge of the cadets and grandees in the service of the Imperial Palace.↩︎
Minister Herald (dàhónglú), one of the Nine Ministers, was in charge of managing ritual protocols in the relations and diplomacy with foreign states and vassal states.↩︎
This refers to Liú Biǎo by his military rank Defending South General (zhènnán jiāngjūn).↩︎
Rǔyáng county was in Rǔnán prefecture.↩︎
Zhānglíng county was in Nányáng prefecture.↩︎
Lì county was in Nányáng prefecture.↩︎
Suburb Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth (jiāosì tiāndì) were an Imperial prerogative. Performing these could be considered a usurpation of Imperial authority.↩︎
Bears (xióngpí) are a metaphor for fierce warriors.↩︎
crumbs: 6  Biographies of Dǒng, Two Yuán, Liú

title: 7  Biographies of Lǚ Bù and Zāng Hóng
text: Lǚ Bù
crumbs: 7  Biographies of Lǚ Bù and Zāng Hóng

title: 7  Biographies of Lǚ Bù and Zāng Hóng
text:
Lǚ Bù appellation Fèngxiān was a Wǔyuán prefecture Jiǔyuán man. For his valor and military ability he served in Bìng Province, the Inspector Dīng Yuán became Cavalry Commandant, garrisoned Hénèi, with [Lǚ] Bù as his Registrar, greatly meeting with close treatment. When Emperor Líng passed away, [Dīng] Yuán led troops to visit Luòyáng, [1] with Hé Jìn plotting to execute the various Yellow Gate, appointed Metal Mace Bearer. [Hé] Jìn was destroyed, Dǒng Zhuó entered the capital city, about to make chaos, wished to kill [Dīng] Yuán, take over his troops and multitudes. [Dǒng] Zhuó because [Lǚ] Bù met with trust from [Dīng] Yuán, enticed [Lǚ] Bù to have him kill [Dīng] Yuán. [Lǚ] Bù cut off [Dīng] Yuán’s head and visited [Dǒng] Zhuó, [Dǒng] Zhuó appointed [Lǚ] Bù as Cavalry Commandant, extremely favored and trusted him, swore to act as father and son.



呂布字奉先，五原郡九原人也。以驍武給并州。刺史丁原為騎都尉，屯河內，以布為主簿，大見親待。靈帝崩，原將兵詣洛陽。〔一〕與何進謀誅諸黃門，拜執金吾。進敗，董卓入京都，將為亂，欲殺原，并其兵眾。卓以布見信于原，誘布令殺原。布斬原首詣卓，卓以布為騎都尉，甚愛信之，誓為父子。










[1] Yīngxióng jì states: [Dīng] Yuán appellation Jiànyáng, originally came from a poor family, as a man was crude and coarse, had military valor, skilled in riding and shooting. Became a Nán county clerk,1 in receiving missions did not decline from difficulties, when there were alarms or emergencies, or pursuit of bandits or caitiffs, then at once he was at the front. He was barely literate, and rarely had clerk duties.



〔一〕　英雄記曰：原子建陽。本出自寒家，為人麤略，有武勇，善騎射。為南縣吏，受使不辭難，有警急，追寇虜，輒在其前。裁知書，少有吏用。







[Lǚ] Bù was skilled with bow and horse, his bodily strength surpassed other men, called as Flying General. Gradually promoted to reach Central Cadet General, enfeoffed a city precinct Marquess. [Dǒng] Zhuó himself knew he treated others without respect, feared others would plot against him, wherever he went or stayed he always had [Lǚ] Bù guard him. However [Dǒng] Zhuó by nature was strong-willed but narrow-minded, in anger did not think of the troubles, once for a small disappointment, he grabbed a hand halberd and threw it at [Lǚ] Bù. [Lǚ] Bù had vigor and speed and dodged it, [2] attended to and apologized to [Dǒng] Zhuó, [Dǒng] Zhuó’s thoughts also resolved. Because of this he secretly hated [Dǒng] Zhuó. [Dǒng] Zhuó always [Lǚ] Bù defend the central boudoirs, [Lǚ] Bù with [Dǒng] Zhuó’s attendant maid had an illicit affair, feared the matter would be discovered, in his heart was not at ease with himself.



布便弓馬，膂力過人，號為飛將。稍遷至中郎將，封都亭侯。卓自以遇人無禮，恐人謀己，行止常以布自衛。然卓性剛而褊，忿不思難，嘗小失意，拔手戟擲布。布拳捷避之，〔一〕為卓顧謝，卓意亦解。由是陰怨卓。卓常使布守中閤，布與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安。










[3] Shī states: “No vigor no valor, precisely a source of chaos.” Annotation states: “Agility is strength.”



〔一〕　詩曰：「無拳無勇，職為亂階。」注：「拳，力也。」







Before this, Excellency over the Masses Wáng Yǔn because [Lǚ] Bù was of the same region and strong and healthy, generously treated and accepted him. Later [Lǚ] Bù visited [Wáng] Yǔn, explained the circumstances of how [Dǒng] Zhuó had almost killed him. At the time [Wáng] Yǔn with Deputy Director Shìsūn Ruì secretly plotted to execute [Dǒng] Zhuó, and therefore informed [Lǚ] Bù to have him be inner assistance. [Lǚ] Bù said: “But we are like father and son!” [Wáng] Yǔn said: “Your natural surname is Lǚ, originally not bone and flesh kin. Now you worry that death will come anytime, what is this talk of father and son?” Lǚ] Bù therefore agreed to it, with his own hand and blade stabbed [Dǒng] Zhuó. The story is in [Dǒng] Zhuó’s biography. [Wáng] Yǔn appointed [Lǚ] Bù as Exerting Warfare General, Lent Stave, rituals comparable to the Three Excellencies, advanced enfeoffment to Marquess of Wēn,2 together maintaining the Court and government. [Lǚ] Bù from since after he killed [Dǒng] Zhuó feared and hated Liáng Province men, the Liáng Province men were all resentful. Because of this Lǐ Jué and others therefore joined together and returned to attack Cháng’ān city. [4] [Lǚ] Bù could not resit, [Lǐ] Jué and the rest therefore entered Cháng’ān. Sixty days after [Dǒng] Zhuó died, [Lǚ] Bù also was defeeated. [5] He led several hundred cavalry out Wǔ Pass, wishing to visit Yuán Shù.



先是，司徒王允以布州里壯健，厚接納之。後布詣允，陳卓幾見殺狀。時允與僕射士孫瑞密謀誅卓，是以告布使為內應。布曰：「奈如父子何！」允曰：「君自姓呂，本非骨肉。今憂死不暇，何謂父子？」布遂許之，手刃刺卓。語在卓傳。允以布為（奮威）〔奮武〕將軍，假節，儀比三司，進封溫侯，共秉朝政。布自殺卓後，畏惡涼州人，涼州人皆怨。由是李傕等遂相結還攻長安城。〔一〕布不能拒，傕等遂入長安。卓死後六旬，布亦敗。〔二〕將數百騎出武關，欲詣袁術。

〔一〕　英雄記曰：郭汜在城北。布開城門，將兵就汜，言「且卻兵，但身決勝負」。汜、布乃獨共對戰，布以矛刺中汜，汜後騎遂前救汜，汜、布遂各兩罷。

[Lǚ] Bù himself believed that by killing [Dǒng] Zhuó he had avenged [Yuán] Shù and wished to be repaid for it. [Yuán] Shù hated his going back and forth, refused and would not receive him. [Lǚ] Bù had a good horse called Chìtù,3 [6] always with his close intimates Chéng Lián, Wèi Yuè and others pierced vanguards and charged formations, and therefore defeated [Zhāng] Yān’s army. 布自以殺卓為術報讎，欲以德之。術惡其反覆，拒而不受。北詣袁紹，紹與布擊張燕于常山。燕精兵萬餘，騎數千。布有良馬曰赤兔。〔一〕常與其親近成廉、魏越等陷鋒突陳，遂破燕軍。而求益兵眾，將士鈔掠，紹患忌之。布覺其意，從紹求去。紹恐還為己害，遣壯士夜掩殺布，不獲。事露，布走河內，〔二〕與張楊合。紹令眾追之，皆畏布，莫敢逼近者。〔三〕

〔二〕　英雄記曰：布自以有功于袁氏，輕傲紹下諸將，以為擅相署置，不足貴也。布求還洛，紹假布領司隸校尉。外言當遣，內欲殺布。明日當發，紹遣甲士三十人，辭以送布。布使止于帳側，偽使人于帳中鼓箏。紹兵臥，布無何出帳去，而兵不覺。夜半兵起，亂斫布床被，謂為已死。明日，紹訊問，知布尚在，乃閉城門。布遂引去。
